The Earth's climate is constantly evolving, driven by a complex interplay of factors. Observing and analyzing these changes from a satellite perspective is crucial to gain a deeper understanding of our planet. Earth observation satellite data hold immense potential for groundbreaking discoveries, yet the sheer volume of data poses significant challenges in data management, processing, and analysis. The advent of artificial intelligence offers a promising solution to unlock the full benefits of these datasets, which would otherwise remain underutilized. In this context, we present EarthNets, a comprehensive end-to-end framework designed to facilitate the integration of AI technology into Earth monitoring initiatives. Our framework comprises three core components: NetStore, NetProces, and NetViewer, which work in tandem to provide a robust and efficient AI platform for Earth observation. A real-world case study showcases the practical applications and effectiveness of EarthNets, which can be easily adapted to various satellite data and environmental monitoring applications. As an open-source resource, EarthNets is freely available for researchers and developers to build upon, further advancing the use of AI in Earth observation. The source code is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/zhongchí/EarthNets. This report presents initial findings obtained through the Vandoorm dataset vali-dation exercise. The dataset is specifically designed for recognition in technical documents, featuring unique challenges such as font variations and vector graphics. We have conducted an initial assessment of pre-trained models like ImageNet and OpenImages, as well as custom-trained models for technical images, and found that training on relevant datasets yields superior results. We have also explored the application of partial fine-tuning and transfer learning for improved performance. Notably, our results demonstrate that dedicated training on technical datasets outstrips the capabilities of models trained on natural images. This research aims to address this knowledge gap by examining ideal regulation principles in the context of complex systems. A methodical approach is proposed to identify and create ideal regulation principles that can be applied to design effective policies for risk assessment and decision-making. This research is grounded in theoretical computer science and is applied to risk assessment and security research, demonstrating its practical applications. A specific example illustrates the process of identifying ideal regulation principles in the context of a specific problem, validating the proposed approach. This research contributes to the field of designing and creating self-regulating systems, yet acknowledges the limitations and encourages further investigation. This work is an initial step towards a systematic method for designing and verifying ideal regulation principles. Ultimately, this research aims to facilitate the design and development of design and automated tools for regulation principles in complex systems. A novel approach to film restoration is presented, leveraging a large-scale temporal model to capture the changing characteristics of film over time. This method employs a gradient-based forward transmission framework, where the input image is progressively sent through an iterative neural network process, both forward and backward in time. This design enables the recovery of a pristine film sequence by removing degradation while maintaining image details. Notably, our framework allows the input of only a single frame, rather than multiple frames, and can effectively handle scenarios where film parameters are unknown. Our model is trained using a loss function that incorporates both film and restoration quality, and we demonstrate its success on both synthetic and real-world degraded temporal film restorations. Our results indicate that it outperforms existing methods, both objectively and subjectively. Notably, we are the first to tackle this challenging problem. Our project code is available on GitHub. Video restorations can be seen on our website. The vulnerability of DNN models to malicious backdoors poses a significant security risk. Existing backdoor attacks are often designed to trigger recognizable responses, making them easily detectable by model owners. Our research introduces an undirected backdoor technique that conceals its trigger by producing ambiguous responses, making it difficult for owners to identify and recover the hidden backdoor even upon reevaluation. This innovative approach involves embedding a complex trigger classifier into the backdoor target, allowing the model to generate inconsistent triggers that are difficult to decipher. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this subtle backdoor attack in producing high backdoor attack rates, even on large-scale datasets. Furthermore, we evaluated the difficulty of identifying backdoors in use and found that the top-performing methods struggle to recover the hidden backdoor with high accuracy, especially when deployed in real-world scenarios. This study also explores the potential of backdoor attacks as a robust intellectual property protection mechanism for datasets. By using backdoors to protect data ownership, we can create a mechanism to safeguard dataset rights and detect copyright infringement. Our experiments show that this approach can effectively identify the use of unlicensed datasets in real-world applications. While the untargeted backdoor attack has limitations, it can be combined with other methods to create a powerful dataset protection mechanism. This research has implications for the development of more sophisticated intellectual property protection solutions, especially in the context of deep learning. The proposed backdoor-based approach can be integrated with existing techniques to create a robust dataset protection platform. Our work also highlights the importance of addressing the security concerns associated with the use of deep learning in real-world applications. A novel error bound, the Chernoff bound, has been developed for a tensor amplifier method based on operator product states. This new bound can be computed in polynomial time and outperforms existing error bounds for local quantum tensor product codes. We introduce the concept of the T-product tensor amplifier and show that it surpasses the performance of the operator product state tensor amplifier. Additionally, we provide a method to simulate the T-product tensor amplifier on near-term quantum devices. This simulation method can be executed using a classical simulator combined with a series of quantum circuits to achieve a higher rate than the operator product state tensor amplifier. Moreover, we present a method to reduce the number of quantum circuits needed for the simulation by optimizing the simulation parameters. Finally, we provide a comparison of the T-product tensor amplifier's performance with that of the operator product state tensor amplifier. Our results demonstrate that the T-product tensor amplifier can achieve a higher rate while maintaining the same local error rate as the operator product state tensor amplifier for a fixed number of quantum systems. This makes the T-product tensor amplifier a promising candidate for near-term quantum channel capacity experiments. A near-term experiment has been proposed to test the T-product tensor amplifier's performance against the operator product state tensor amplifier. This experiment has the potential to demonstrate the T-product tensor amplifier's ability to achieve a higher rate while maintaining the same local error rate as the operator product state tensor amplifier for a fixed number of quantum systems. The experiment involves measuring the fidelity of the T-product tensor amplifier and the operator product state tensor amplifier under the same conditions of quantum systems and error rates. If successful, this experiment will be the first demonstration of the T-product tensor amplifier's ability to achieve a higher rate while maintaining the same local error rate as the operator product state tensor amplifier for a fixed number of quantum systems. The demonstration of the T-product tensor amplifier's performance will be a significant step towards the experimental realization of the quantum channel capacity theorem. This achievement will be a major milestone in the field of quantum information theory. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive review of the mathematical framework for tensor product amplifiers. This review provides a clear and concise introduction to the mathematical concepts necessary to understand the T-product tensor amplifier. This introduction is suitable for readers who are new to the field of tensor product amplifiers. Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of the mathematical structure of the T-product tensor amplifier. This analysis is a comprehensive treatment of the mathematical structure necessary to understand the T-product tensor amplifier. This comprehensive treatment is a major contribution to the field of quantum information theory.

This study presents a comprehensive framework for extracting and classifying
narrative content from various media formats. The narrative extraction process
involves breaking down text into fundamental components, such as core
narrative elements and supporting narrative units, which are then used to
construct a narrative tree. To classify a given text as a novel, movie synopsis, or
commentary, we employ machine learning algorithms to analyze the extracted
features. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in
identifying and isolating narrative content within a large dataset of text
samples. We also discuss potential applications of this method in real-world
scenarios. The source code and sample dataset are available on GitHub.

In the context of Newman-Penrose formalism, bivectors play a pivotal role in the representation of electromagnetic field modes. Expanding on this concept, the field mode structure is developed to describe the Weyl curvature tensor, revealing an analogous mode structure in electro-magnetic and gravitational fields. Furthermore, the relationship between the mode structure of Weyl's second invariant and Newman-Penrose's spinor representation of Riemannian curvature is examined, with a discussion on potential applications to gravitational data analysis. An analysis of the null-tetrad components of the wave operator is presented, along with a derivation of the relationship between Weyl's invariants and Newman-Penrose's spinor representation of these invariants. An example of constructing the Weyl tensor from Newman-Penrose's spinor representation is also provided. Finally, the discussion concludes with a reflection on the potential implications of these findings for gravitational wave research. In a shared environment, we examine a selection process for K items where each item is evaluated by the server based on its initial characteristics. The client then receives feedback in the form of comparison outcomes from the server, allowing it to decide whether to accept or reject the item for testing. We propose an algorithm, adaptive DART, which maximizes the expected number of selected items for a given client interaction budget by optimizing acceptance decisions adaptively. We derive a lower bound for the algorithm's expected performance and demonstrate that its expected value converges to the optimal outcome at a rate of $O(1/\sqrt{KNT})$. Moreover, we show that adaptive DART surpasses a previously established non-adaptive method in expected performance. To validate our findings, we test DART in a real-world application using a large dataset, revealing that DART outperforms a baseline method in identifying top-K items. Specifically, DART outperforms the baseline method by 20-70% in identifying top-K items. We also observe that DART outperforms the previously established non-linear method in identifying top-K items. Finally, we apply DART to a real-world application, the top-10 in-situ learning algorithm, and demonstrate that DART outperforms the baseline method by 20-40%. The results also show that DART outperforms the previously established non-linear method by 5-40%. Overall, our results demonstrate that adaptive DART is a more efficient method for selecting the top-K items in a shared environment. Significant advancements in neural abstractive summarization have been achieved by pre-trained language models, which however are prone to generating summaries that contain fabricated or misleading information. To mitigate this issue, researchers have developed summary quality evaluation metrics that are susceptible to biases present in training data and evaluation datasets. Our proposed solution, TES, is a metric that promotes factual accuracy in summaries by pre-training on a gold standard dataset of factually accurate summaries. TES also incorporates a unique penalty for out-of-coverage text to counter potential biases. Our results show that TES outperforms leading metrics in identifying truthful summaries and results in loyal summaries that remain faithful to the original documents. The Semantic Web has successfully implemented the RDF model, enabling the representation of vast amounts of data in a structured graph format. Standardized query languages such as SPARQL allow users to access and manipulate these graphs via a common language interface. However, these languages have a limitation in handling visual media data, a significant shortcoming given the increasing adoption of multimedia technologies. To address this issue, we propose VGStore, a novel extension to SPARQL that empowers the use of visual media data, by converting RDF graph data into a Visual Graph Description Language (VGDL) format, a unifying language for visual media data. This results in a more comprehensive graph structure, incorporating visual media data, ultimately leading to a unified query language, VGQuery. A visual simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) algorithm's performance can be optimized by leveraging its global localization (GL) function to improve loop closures, which in turn boosts accuracy and reduces errors. Although GL visually verifies the algorithm's ability to locally localize, it does not solely guarantee loop closure, which is also facilitated through other methods. In this study, we present a novel bi-directional circuit closure system that leverages visual cues and probabilistic models to reliably detect loops. Our system's GL stage employs a probabilistic model to estimate potential loop connections and generate a list of probable matches. Subsequently, the loop closure stage utilizes visual features to confirm these potential matches, thus completing a bi-directional circuit closure. Our system's effectiveness is demonstrated through both simulated and real-world experiments, which reveal that it achieves loop closures at 99.9% and 100.0% accuracy in simulation and real scenarios, respectively. Moreover, our system's application on a robot empowers it to operate in unknown environments for extended durations without experiencing localization failures. This research tackles the formation tracking problem with a group of agents in the form of rigid and articulated bodies in the presence of unknown external influences in networks with directed connections. A novel bearing-based approach is proposed to achieve formation with a moving leader node using sliding-mode regulation rules that prioritize bearing information. These rules are specifically designed for bearing-only state feedback in the case of rigid bodies, and for bearing and velocity information in the case of articulated bodies. A key contribution of this research is the derivation of sliding-mode regulation rules that do not rely on the estimation of the relative dynamics or the leader's dynamics. A theoretical analysis confirms the proposed controllers' ability to achieve asymptotic convergence of the group's formation with a desired error bound, and simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of these controllers in both scenarios. The findings of this research are supported by a comparison with existing bearing-only formation controllers and a method that relies on velocity information. The results show that the proposed controllers achieve comparable performance to the velocity-based method while not requiring velocity information. Moreover, the proposed controllers' ability to reject disturbances and track the leader's trajectory is superior to the bearing-only formation controller. A comparative analysis of the proposed controllers' performance is also conducted with respect to different network connectivity and communication delays. The results show that the proposed controllers achieve a high degree of robustness in the presence of these factors. Ultimately, the proposed controllers' performance is evaluated in a scenario where the leader node is replaced by a moving target, and the results show that the group's formation is successfully achieved. Generative Adversarial Networks generate high-quality images through a process of min-max optimization between two interconnected neural networks. However, this process is often hindered by a phenomenon known as mode collapse, which occurs when the networks fail to explore the full range of the distribution, resulting in the creation of only a limited number of images. Previous research has attempted to understand mode collapse through the analysis of generated samples and network parameters, but these methods lack a clear theoretical explanation for the occurrence. This study proposes an innovative approach to diagnosing mode collapse by examining Hessian eigenvalues, which provide insight into the optimization landscape of the min-max problem. We demonstrate that our method effectively detects mode collapse in three distinct scenarios: initial training, convergence, and premature convergence. Furthermore, we show that our method is more effective than a widely used mode collapse detection method based on visual similarity metrics. Our findings suggest that mode collapse occurs when the Hessian eigenvalues, indicative of the optimization gradient, drops to zero, leading to a stagnant optimization process. Additionally, we found that mode collapse is more prevalent in scenarios involving the use of small batch sizes and early stopping. Our study's results are consistent with the Hessian analysis, providing new insights into the optimization landscape of the min-max problem. Overall, this study offers a novel diagnostic tool for detecting mode collapse in generative adversarial networks. The accompanying code for this study is available at https://github.com/taofindgans. Social media platforms are plagued by the widespread dissemination of false information, which can be exploited to manipulate public opinion. To counteract this issue, researchers have developed methods to identify and debunk false news, but their effectiveness is hindered by the scarcity of high-quality training data. To address this limitation, we propose an innovative approach to automatically generate a large dataset of false news articles, which can be used to supplement existing datasets and improve the performance of false news detection algorithms. Our experiment demonstrates that models trained on this synthetic data can achieve comparable results to those trained on existing datasets, but only when the training data includes a range of false news styles. However, the generated data is not as effective when models are evaluated on unseen datasets with different stylistic characteristics. To overcome this limitation, we propose a hybrid approach that combines generated data with human-annotated data, which can be used to develop more robust false news detection algorithms. Our experiments demonstrate that this hybrid approach outperforms models trained on generated data and achieves comparable results to those trained on human-annotated data, suggesting that generated data can be a valuable resource for improving false news detection. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach can be applied to other natural language processing tasks, such as hate speech detection. Our work provides a foundation for the development of more accurate and robust false news detection algorithms, which can be achieved by combining synthetic data with human annotations. The Coefficient Inverse Scattering Problem involves numerically reconstructing a high-dimensional, unknown coefficient from a single measurement of the associated nonlocal differential equation, which is highly complex and nonlinear. We apply a non-iterative, convexification approach for numerical inversion using a nonlinear, non-convex least squares objective function, incorporating a nonlocal, non-convex penalty term to ensure the coefficient's non-negativity. We validate the proposed method using numerical experiments in 2-D and 3-D space, demonstrating its ability to accurately reconstruct the coefficient. To assess the effectiveness and robustness of our approach, we also investigate its sensitivity to noise in the measurement data. Our results demonstrate the potential of convexification techniques for solving complex inverse problems in high-dimensional scenarios. This research has implications for various applications, including inverse problems in atmospheric scattering, neutron transport, and geophysical phenomena. The goal of image pan-sharpening is to combine low-resolution and multispectral images into a single high-resolution image containing spectral data, while maintaining spatial information. Traditional methods for pan-sharpening typically involve two stages: first, a feature extraction process using a deep neural network, and second, a reconstruction process using hand-designed filters. However, these two stages are often optimized separately, leading to inconsistent results. In this research, a new approach called Gradient Projection Networks (GPNs) is proposed to integrate spectral and spatial information in a single network. GPNs achieve this by projecting the feature extraction network's output onto a high-resolution image, using hand-designed filters as constraints. This allows the network to learn optimal filters for feature extraction, resulting in improved image fusion. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of GPNs, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods for pan-sharpening. GPNs are also shown to be computationally efficient, making them a promising approach for future research in this field. Furthermore, we leverage this result to derive new findings, including a novel technique to identify the smallest degree polynomials within irreducible complex representations of GL(n) and a novel characterization of the highest weight vectors within specific irreducible representations of GL(n) over finite fields. Notably, our investigation reveals that these vectors cannot be explicitly described through the use of polynomials. Additionally, we demonstrate that our technique can be adapted to other reductive and reductive with torus, specifically SL(2), GL(3), and SU(n) for n ≥ 3. In human-robot collaboration, a key challenge lies in determining which tasks to hand off to a robot, balancing the robot's processing capabilities with the human's available resources. We investigated how humans make this decision by creating a framework that simulates task assignment, where humans evaluate and compare tasks based on computational load and utility. We discovered that humans break down tasks in accordance with a simple decision rule: they prioritize tasks with the highest marginal value per processing requirement, applying this rule recursively until the task cannot be further divided. This approach effectively captures human task-handoff strategies, demonstrating that humans efficiently allocate tasks to minimize overall processing expense while maximizing utility. Additionally, our framework can be used to predict human task assignments and even identify when a task cannot be divided, all while respecting human resource constraints. By integrating this knowledge into collaborative robotics systems, these robots can better handle task allocation and processing. Ultimately, this research provides insights to inform the design of future collaborative robots that work closely with humans. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ISLET by comparing it to 11 state-of-the-art methods on 10 real-world datasets and verify its superiority in terms of both speed and prediction accuracy. Moreover, a theoretical analysis confirms that ISLET's convergence performance is on par with the current best convergence results for stochastic optimization. In addition, we conduct a comprehensive sensitivity analysis to identify the optimal parameters for ISLET and highlight the key factors that impact its performance. Experimental results show that ISLET's efficiency and accuracy make it an attractive choice for tensor regression tasks. Specifically, it can achieve up to 30 times faster convergence than the best baseline method while maintaining comparable accuracy. We believe that ISLET's innovative approach to low-rank tensor regression will open up new possibilities for the efficient analysis of large tensor datasets. To further improve performance, AttDLNet incorporates an attention mechanism that dynamically prioritizes the most informative features. Experimental results demonstrate that AttDLNet significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency, establishing new benchmarks in the field. We have made our code publicly available to facilitate future research. In the context of machine learning, data privacy concerns a significant issue, and  differential privacy offers a robust framework to ensure sensitive data information is protected.  However, existing studies have found that differential privacy may compromise model performance, and thus a balance needs to be struck between data protection and model accuracy. This research examines the trade-off between differential privacy and regularization techniques in optimization problems, and how they impact model performance, using tools from convex analysis. We explore existing relationships between differential privacy and regularization, and demonstrate that differential privacy can be viewed as an alternative regularization method that offers additional benefits, such as improved generalization and robustness against overfitting. Our findings suggest that differential privacy can actually enhance model performance in certain cases, and may even be a viable alternative to traditional regularization techniques in specific situations. We also propose a novel approach to combining differential privacy with regularization, and demonstrate that this hybrid method can lead to improved model performance and robustness. This research provides valuable insights into the relationship between differential privacy and regularization in optimization problems, and may be of interest to practitioners working in machine learning.  The code for this research is available at https://github.com/taohuangACIT/DP-Optimization.  To make our findings more accessible to practitioners, we have also developed a visualization tool to help users understand the impact of differential privacy on model performance, and to provide guidance on how to strike a balance between data protection and model accuracy in real-world applications.  This tool is available at https://public.italianmaru.com/DP-Optimization.  We hope that this research will contribute to a deeper understanding of the relationship between differential privacy and regularization in optimization problems, and will inspire the development of new approaches to protect sensitive data information while maintaining model performance.  The findings of this research are also relevant to practitioners working in optimization problems, and we hope that they will be of use to them in their future research. The geoscience field is experiencing a significant impact from the increasing availability of large datasets, which has led to breakthroughs in areas such as oil and gas resource recovery, climate modeling, and system monitoring on a global scale. This surge in data is attributed to advancements in both data collection systems and storage capabilities. However, it presents a major challenge to process and interpret these vast datasets in a timely manner. In response, deep learning methods have emerged as a promising solution for extracting valuable information from these datasets, particularly in the context of spatio-temporal modeling. This study focuses on applying a novel 4D seismic monitoring technique for CO2 storage by leveraging a hybrid generative-conversational approach. By integrating CNNs with time-series analysis, we have developed an in-situ system that can identify CO2 storage anomalies from field data, reducing the need for sophisticated 4D seismic processing pipelines. Our proposed approach has demonstrated exceptional accuracy in detecting CO2 storage anomalies, with an average F1 score of 0.96, and outperforms established baseline models in multiple evaluations. Moreover, our end-to-end learning framework enables seamless deployment on edge devices, facilitating real-time monitoring and analysis of CO2 storage data. The rapid growth of mobile devices and IoT sensors has led to a substantial increase in the volume of raw data, necessitating the use of big data management systems that can handle this data effectively.  Multi-agent systems, particularly those based on JADE, have been widely used to address complex issues in real-time environments.  However, the limited processing power of agent-dynamics and traditional architectures often results in performance degradation and scalability challenges.  To address this issue, this study proposes a novel framework, PASCAL, which leverages in-memory computing and agent-evolution to create a persistent and scalable multi-agent system.  PASCAL employs a unique agent-evolution model, incorporating the concept of agent migration to optimize system performance, and incorporates in-memory computing to enhance agent evolution efficiency.  Additionally, the framework utilizes a data management system to store agent states and facilitate agent migration, thus ensuring system persistence.  Experimental results demonstrate that PASCAL outperforms traditional JADE in terms of scalability, achieving a 2.5 times faster evolution rate and a 2.3 times higher agent population, while also ensuring system persistence.  The study also highlights the practical applications of PASCAL in real-world scenarios, such as IoT data collection and cloud-based healthcare systems.  Code for PASCAL is available on GitHub. This study focuses on calculating the dimensions of subgroups associated with a 2-stage nilpotent Lie group and draws connections to Lie algebras. We explore a specific family of Lie groups that are extensions of split Heisenberg Lie groups over real numbers. By establishing a canonical projection map, we develop a method for identifying free and normal subgroups within these Lie groups. We also provide a detailed description of their geometric structure, including a canonical connection and related horocycles, and calculate their bi-invariant metrics. Recent research has highlighted the significant vulnerability of deep neural networks to adversarial attacks that manipulate their behavior on specific classes without the adversary's knowledge. This study delves into a related issue: can an adversary introduce a backdoor into a pre-trained neural network by modifying its weights? The answer is negative, as our research demonstrates that manipulating a neural network's weights to trigger a backdoor is impossible. This is because the relationship between a network's output and its weight values is highly non-linear, making it impossible for an adversary to accurately predict the output based on weight alterations. authentication models that can learn from data without pre-defined parameters.
We developed a trainable equivalent to the standard 13-dimensional Mel-frequency
cepstral coefficient, which we call trainable MFCC, and tested it in an
experiment where it was used in conjunction with a deep neural network to
identify speakers. We observed that using the trainable MFCC results in improved
identification rates compared to traditional Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients.
We also investigated how different coefficient training methods impact speaker
recognition and found that only coefficient regularization yields better
performance than the original MFCC system. Furthermore, we found that applying
regularization to the trainable MFCC coefficient leads to improved speaker
recognition. Notably, our experiments showed that using the trainable MFCC in
conjunction with a speaker adaptation method enables the re-training of speaker
models without relying on mel-spectra, which are often difficult to generate.
The proposed trainable MFCC framework allows for more flexible training of speech
representation models and can be applied to various speech processing tasks. The

The ability to read, visualize, and write code is fundamental to software developers, yet relatively little research has been conducted on how these skills are processed in the brain. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted a neuroimaging study with 46 participants learning the basics of programming through either text or interactive visualization. To gain deeper insights, we also collected data on their performance and emotional responses. By analyzing the brain activity of healthy participants using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), we discovered that reading, visualizing, and writing code engage distinct neural networks. Notably, we found that programming activates brain regions involved in language processing, spatial navigation, and control. Furthermore, we observed significant differences in neural activity and emotional responses between text-based and interactive learning formats, and found that our findings are consistent regardless of participants' prior programming experience. This groundbreaking study offers a comprehensive understanding of the neural processes that underlie programming skills and sheds light on the benefits and trade-offs of different learning approaches. Ultimately, our research has the potential to inform the development of more effective programming instruction and support for individuals learning to program. Ultimately, we discuss the implications of these findings on $DR$'s validity in real-world applications. Most existing methods address this issue by modeling the transmission with a single neural network, yet this approach is inefficient as it requires a large number of parameters. To overcome this limitation, our approach proposes a novel transmission estimation strategy, which leverages a distillation-based method to learn the transmission map from hazy images with high clarity, such as those captured using a haze filter, and the resulting dehazed images. This method is effective in learning the transmission map from images with high clarity, and we further enhance it by introducing a feature connection module to learn the transmission map from both clear and dehazed images. Our approach is evaluated on both synthetic and real-world datasets, yielding state-of-the-art results. In distributed support vector machines, parallel implementation through gradient descent is common, but this often leads to slow convergence due to the need to recompute complex kernel functions. We introduce a groundbreaking, self-supervised method for image denoising that 
utilizes a unique dual approach. Firstly, it creates a controlled disturbance in the
image using a series of random masks, and secondly, it employs a form of regularization 
through a novel dual-loss strategy, where one loss term encourages the restored image 
to closely resemble the original non-noisy image, while the other term promotes the restored 
image to closely resemble the artificially noisy image. This approach, dubbed Decay2Distill, 
does not rely on any supervised content data and can effectively restore high-quality images 
without any notable content degradation. Our proposed method has been extensively tested on a wide 
range of natural images and outperforms state-of-the-art supervised and self-supervised denoising techniques. 
Notably, it has been shown to effectively preserve delicate details, such as textures and lines, in the restored images. 
Additionally, it has been successfully applied to the challenging task of removing banding artifacts from JPEG 
compressed images, yielding superior results. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub for further review.

Deep learning models are widely used in various applications, such as facial recognition, medical image analysis, and image captioning, but their reliance on pre-trained features from related tasks also brings a hidden risk of backdoor attacks. These attacks involve compromising model accuracy on legitimate data and artificially high error rates on targeted backdoor examples, which could have severe implications for applications like facial recognition. To address this issue, we introduce a novel defense mechanism that can detect and counter backdoor instances in facial recognition tasks. We first identify the optimal trigger pattern in facial images and create backdoor instances. We then develop a defense mechanism using a discriminator to detect backdoor inputs and utilize a trigger extractor to eliminate the backdoor trigger in tested images. We test our method on several datasets and show its effectiveness in countering backdoor attacks. We also test our method on real-world datasets and find that it can accurately identify backdoor inputs and outperform existing methods. Moreover, our method does not require retraining of the facial recognition model, making it a practical solution for real-world applications. We demonstrate the security and efficiency of our method through extensive experiments. We also provide a warning to the public about the potential risks of backdoor attacks on facial recognition systems and the need for a robust defense mechanism. Galaxy groups are a valuable resource for studying cosmology due to their extensive spatial scale, high frequency of occurrence, and relatively low susceptibility to environmental influences. However, their utility in cosmological research is hindered by the need for accurate mass estimations, which are often hampered by the subjective nature of halo definition criteria and the necessity for precise mass-to-light ratio estimations. Moreover, observational cosmology is further complicated by the requirement for correcting galaxy luminosity functions across diverse redshift ranges. The primary objective of this study is to investigate the occurrence of transits within a subset of {\delta} Scuti stars observed by the Kepler space telescope. Utilizing a customized version of the {\tt TESS Data Analysis Tool}, an established machine learning technique, a light curve inversion was performed to identify periodic variations. It is hypothesized that transits in this class of stars may be more prevalent than previously acknowledged. Diabetic foot ulcers are a major complication affecting approximately 460 million diabetics, resulting in around 500,000 amputations every year worldwide, of which nearly 160,000 occur in the Americas. DFU patients often experience delayed medical treatment due to difficulties in identifying the condition from low-quality images. This research aims to address this issue by developing a deep learning-based medical imaging analysis tool that enhances low-resolution images of diabetic foot ulcers, facilitating early DFU detection and prevention of unnecessary complications. Our proposed approach involves a two-stage process that includes a U-Net for super resolution image enhancement and noise suppression using the U-Net and Autoencoder architectures. We evaluated our methods' performance by comparing the enhanced images with both original low-resolution and SR images, as well as assessing the efficiency of noise suppression using the U-Net and Autoencoder models. Our findings indicate that the SR model achieved a 2.5-fold reduction in missing lesions and a 2.8-fold reduction in false positives when analyzing enhanced images. Moreover, our noise suppression models achieved a 2.3-fold reduction in false positives when compared to the original low-resolution images. This research has significant implications for early DFU diagnosis, potentially leading to substantial reductions in related amputations and mortality rates. We anticipate that our methods will contribute to improved medical image analysis in the future. By leveraging pre-existing language models, our system can accurately transcribe speech into written text for languages previously unexplored in the deep learning field. We've also demonstrated the effectiveness of our method in improving the recognition capabilities of existing language models, by fine-tuning the model using a small data set of just 20 seconds of speech. To validate our model's potential for broader language coverage, we've successfully applied it to test data from an unknown language, while also publicly releasing our code to enable others to build upon and expand upon our work. Furthermore, we've identified potential areas for improvement and outline the avenues for future investigation. Federated learning in deep neural networks enables collaborative model training on disparate datasets to occur without data exchange. A significant limitation of FL lies in its reliance on a shared global model that gets updated based on the performance of the entire distributed training group. This often results in models that are sub-optimally tailored to individual datasets, reducing their efficiency. This paper presents an innovative FL approach, dubbed "Federated Customized Training" (FCT), which leverages hypernetworks to address this issue. Unlike traditional FL methods that rely on a single model updated across all participants, FCT allows each participant to train a custom model tailored to their dataset, using a hypernetwork that generates the model based on the client's specific task. This approach eliminates the need for global model updates and enables each participant to develop a personalized model that outperforms the shared global model. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of FCT using the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets. Notably, FCT can reduce top-1 error rates by up to 24% and 3% or achieve a 2x to 4x reduction in training iterations compared to traditional FL methods while maintaining comparable communication costs. A publicly available implementation of FCT can be accessed at https://github.com/zhirongbai/FCT. The code is available under the MIT license. We introduce a novel method for generating sound waves using stochastic differential equations. This method utilizes a random It\^o differential equation to drive wave propagation and demonstrates its ability to produce a wide range of sound wave forms, from simple sinusoids to complex signals. By leveraging this stochastic wave generation technique, we can synthesize novel sounds that are distinct from existing ones, thus expanding a model's sonic capabilities. We showcase the efficacy of this method by applying it to a model of a freely-ribsuspended membrane and also develop a parameterized family of stochastic waveforms that can be used with any wave equation. This method is made more efficient by incorporating techniques such as preconditioning and diagonal shift. We demonstrate the diversity of sound waveforms produced by our model and also show that our approach can be extended to higher-dimensional domains. In addition to audio examples, the sound waveforms produced by our model are visualized. We also provide source code for reproducing our results and for generating sound waveforms. Overall, our work provides a new perspective on stochastic wave production and opens up new possibilities for the field of sonic research. We hope that this work will inspire a new generation of creative modelers to explore the vast sonic possibilities that are waiting to be discovered. This study introduces a pioneering deep learning model that utilizes audio input to diagnose COVID-19 respiratory sounds. By leveraging pre-trained deep learning models and specialized audio processing techniques, our model can accurately identify COVID-19 from respiratory sounds. We developed a novel model, COVID-gram, which enhances the pre-trained Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC) feature extraction process through a two-stage transformer architecture. Notably, COVID-gram outperforms existing state-of-the-art models on the COVID-19 Sound Dataset, achieving a remarkable ROC-AUC of 0.9132 while maintaining a relatively low number of parameters. Furthermore, our model demonstrates exceptional generalizability by performing competitively on the PULM COVID-19 dataset with only 100 training samples. Our findings indicate that audio input can be a valuable tool in detecting COVID-19, and we envision that this model, along with other sound-based detection methods, can be an effective means of identifying COVID-19 in resource-constrained areas. We investigate the issue of minimizing the expected response time for a collection of independent queueing systems that process tasks with varying arrival rates and service times drawn from distinct, exponentially modulated distributions. This problem is encountered in scenarios such as load balancing in cloud computing, crowdsourcing, grid computing, and virtual networks. To address this challenge, we develop a method that yields an exact solution with a doubly exponential bound on the optimal response time. Our approach relies on a closed-form approximation for the second-order PASTA factor, which is derived using a step-by-step analytical method, and subsequently used to establish a doubly exponential lower bound on the optimal response time. This bound can be computed in under one second, allowing for its practical application in settings where an optimal solution is not feasible due to excessive computational requirements. Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficacy of our method by applying it to a variety of load balancing scenarios, including both single-server and multiple-server systems, with different load distributions. Our findings show that the method produces accurate estimates of the optimal response time, outperforming a previously known heuristic method by an order of magnitude, while also being more efficient than exact simulation methods. Moreover, we demonstrate that the optimal solution exhibits a high degree of robustness, with minor changes in the optimal response time in the face of significant changes to the load distribution. This work provides a novel solution to a long-standing challenge in the field, offering significant practical implications for load balancing. As neural network designs evolve, we can leverage existing architectures by exploring the vast design space, identifying key features that enhance performance, reliability, and efficiency. To accomplish this, designers employ gradient-based search methods, generating new models through iterative steps. However, this process can be time-consuming and resource-intensive. In this research, we propose an approach to analyze the design space of deep neural networks by employing dimensionality reduction and clustering methods. The widespread adoption of smart meters in the Internet of Things (IoT) has led to concerns about data security and privacy, which is further complicated by the limited computational power and storage capacity of these devices. This paper presents a lightweight and safe network authentication system (LiSA) specifically designed to meet the stringent security and privacy requirements of smart meters. By utilizing a 160-bit security level, LiSA incorporates identity-based authentication protocols and achieves enhanced security and efficiency. A key feature of LiSA is its ability to utilize pre-shared secrets and publicly available information to generate multi-factor credentials, thereby ensuring robustness against various types of attacks. Moreover, LiSA boasts improved efficiency and flexibility while ensuring strong security and privacy properties. To validate the feasibility of LiSA, a prototype was developed and successfully implemented on a Raspberry Pi board. Experimental results indicate that LiSA can be easily deployed on resource-constrained devices with a power consumption of just 31.45mW. Finally, LiSA outperforms existing systems in terms of security, privacy, flexibility, and power consumption. Go's growing popularity as a concurrent systems programming language necessitates a method for detecting and validating concurrent programs' expected behavior. Currently available Go program verifiers focus on ensuring safety, but less attention has been given to identifying concurrency defects, specifically race conditions. Our research introduces binGo, a tool that uses binary examination to identify race conditions in Go programs by exploiting the Go compiler's features. By converting Go source code into an intermediate representation, binGo detects race conditions without source code access, which allows it to identify a significant number of race conditions in widely used Go packages. Our results show that binGo outperforms existing tools, such as Go itself, while also being more effective at detecting race conditions than a previous tool. Furthermore, our evaluation reveals that binGo detects a substantial proportion of race conditions in Go programs. Our study also demonstrates the potential of using binary examination for Go compiler analysis, which could lead to future improvements. This study presents a novel approach to COVID-19 modeling, leveraging a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm (QB-MI) that integrates machine learning techniques with quantum insights. The proposed framework, QB-MI, utilizes a quantum-boosted version of Random Forest machine learning to forecast COVID-19 cases. We apply this methodology to two distinct datasets: the first, a quantum Anderson insulator system, and the second, COVID-19 cases in the United States. Our findings indicate that the QB-MI algorithm effectively captures the underlying quantum behavior of the Anderson insulator system, achieving accuracy rates of 99.2% and 99.3% for different subsets. Furthermore, when applied to COVID-19 data, QB-MI demonstrates superior performance compared to classical machine learning algorithms, yielding a notable 6.5% increase in accuracy. This innovative approach has the potential to be extended to other fields, such as materials science and neuroscience, and could provide a valuable tool for addressing pressing issues like cancer diagnosis and weather forecasting. The methodology's adaptability and efficacy in multiple contexts make it an attractive solution for addressing complex challenges in the physical and medical sciences. In contrast, a significant minority of papers can be classified as "dead-end" research, with authors failing to reference them in subsequent work within three years. The findings suggest that the COVID-19 pandemic has fostered research with practical applications, albeit with a smaller portion of research contributing to ongoing knowledge advancement. These observations have important implications for the evaluation of research productivity and impact. Additional analysis reveals that the COVID-19 pandemic has also had a profound impact on the broader social fabric, with research on mental health and its effects on individuals and society increasing substantially. Furthermore, a significant portion of research on social issues related to the pandemic can be classified as lacking long-term significance. The research also sheds light on the gender dynamics of the research community, with women making up a larger proportion of authors on papers related to the pandemic but receiving fewer citations for their work. These findings have significant implications for the assessment of research productivity and impact, the development of research policies, and broader social issues. Software call graphs are frequently used in various static analysis methods for
program understanding. However, these methods face challenges when analyzing the
evolution of software systems across multiple versions and branches of development.
Current approaches to call graph analysis are often designed to handle a specific
point-in-time snapshot of a program or a limited version history, neglecting the
need for long-term analysis. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel
approach to developing call graphs that can adapt to changing software versions
and needs over time. This approach involves leveraging a type of software change
set, which outlines the specific modifications made to a system at a particular
stage of its development. Using this information, our method can efficiently
generate call graphs that reflect the impact of recent changes. In our initial
test, this approach was applied to the Linux kernel, which has undergone extensive
development, and demonstrated its ability to produce high-quality call graphs that
reflect current understanding and can be further refined as the system evolves,
thereby reducing the need for complete rework in response to future changes. 
The source code for this approach is available online. The results of our analysis
are also provided as supplementary materials. The research described here was
presented at ICSE 2021.

Our method is demonstrated through numerical examples and real-world applications in weather forecasting and climate science. As robots and autonomous systems increasingly integrate into our daily lives,
the need for ensuring their safety has become a pressing concern. Safety
overseers, often in the form of formal verification and certification, aim to
mitigate the risk of system failures by verifying control systems against
specific standards. Although numerous safety overseers have been developed to
address various challenges in robot and autonomous system design, a comprehensive
evaluation of these systems is lacking. This research aims to bridge the gap
by providing an extensive comparison of 20 safety overseers across six key
criteria, including the system's scope, system architecture, verification
approach, deployment criteria, implementation methods, and heuristic search strategies.
This analysis highlights the advantages and limitations of safety overseers, thus
guiding future research directions in this field. Additionally, this study provides
insight into the effectiveness of different safety overseers, which can serve
as a valuable resource for both researchers and industry professionals seeking
innovative solutions in this area. This research is intended to serve as a
significant contribution to the ongoing conversation regarding the development of
safety overseers for robots and autonomous systems. The findings presented here
could potentially spark new discussions and spark further research in this field. 
The accompanying code and datasets are available online at: 
https://github.com/ozan-ozdemir/SA Safety_Overses. 
This study is part of the ongoing PhD research on safety overseers on robots and
autonomous systems at the University of Southern California.

Design, System Architecture, System Design, Control Systems, Verification
Approach, System Implementation, System Deployment, System Search.

Self-supervised learning has made significant progress in visual tasks, but it is still unclear how it is affected by variations in training data. This paper investigates how differences in the distribution of visual data affect the performance of self-supervised models, particularly when comparing datasets that are more similar or dissimilar. Our findings show that these models can still learn effectively from similar datasets but struggle with dissimilar ones, and that this is due to the quality of the representations they produce. Moreover, our results indicate that self-supervised models are less vulnerable to data disparities when compared to supervised models, and that this advantage grows when using more challenging self-supervised learning methods. To address this issue, we propose a technique that improves model robustness by reducing the gap in the visual data distribution. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach leads to better performance for self-supervised models, and that they are able to match the performance of supervised models. Overall, our research highlights the importance of considering dataset disparities in the development of self-supervised learning methods. Additionally, our code is available on GitHub at \url{https://github.com/rahulshah@iitgn.com/self_supervision_disparities}.

Our key findings show that self-supervised models are more robust to dataset shifts compared to supervised models, and that this resilience improves with the difficulty of the self-supervised learning method. Continuous-action reinforcement learning (CARL) is a challenging field due to its non-stationary nature in continuous action spaces and environments. This research addresses the difficulties in finding an optimal policy for continuous control tasks, especially when the environment is dynamic. A key problem is that existing CARL methods are prone to overestimation, which can lead to overconfident policy decisions in uncertain situations. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a new approach, Coordinated Policy Enhancement (CoPee), which combines a risk-sensitive enhancement criterion with a policy optimization method to enhance the quality of learned policies. We evaluate the effectiveness of CoPee on various continuous control tasks, including dynamic challenges and games. Our results show that CoPee outperforms existing CARL methods in terms of efficiency and robustness to non-stationarity, and also demonstrates its potential in solving complex tasks involving interactions with other agents. This research provides a framework for improving policy quality in CARL and also highlights the importance of developing robust policies in dynamic and uncertain environments. CoPee's success in various challenging scenarios and games demonstrates its potential in solving complex tasks, and we believe that this contribution will advance the field of CARL and facilitate future research in this area. FMM enables the creation of accurate synthetic data by modeling the underlying rhythms of the data, allowing for the fitting of a complex mixture model to a given time series. Additionally, we observed that our method allows for more precise control over simulations and enables the identification of key points in energy landscapes. This research demonstrates the potential of a dynamic and adaptive approach to sampling in improving efficiency in complex simulations. The Local Hamiltonian problem is a fundamental challenge in quantum physics, particularly in the study of many-body systems. Our research delves into the complexity of this problem, focusing on its parameterized version that involves a parameter g representing the energy gap between the ground and excited states. We investigate the complexity of this problem for different constraints and show that it can be solved in polynomial time under certain conditions, including local interactions and unique product states. These results demonstrate that the Local Hamiltonian problem is tractable for many physical systems and provide evidence for the Quantum Exponential Time Conjecture. In video communication systems, the prevalent use of lossy video codecs like H.264 and VP9, with subsequent compression, makes the original video data irrecoverable, thus limiting the feasibility of decompression-based methods. To address this issue, we introduce Gemino, an innovative neural compression technique that restores the original video by decompressing the pixel data within a latent space learned via a joint neural autoencoder-decompression model. Initially trained on vast datasets without supervision, this model can effectively reconstruct decoded video data from compressed latent data, with significant improvements in rate-distortion performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, the decompression component of Gemino demonstrates robustness to adversarial attacks, specifically latticetexture attacks, by maintaining its ability to accurately restore video data even when attacked, with minimal degradation in quality. A thorough analysis of Gemino's training and decompression processes is provided, with supporting results from extensive experiments conducted on two prominent datasets, VID4L-2 and KITTI Raw Video, showcasing the system's capabilities. Analyzing high-dimensional time series data with a small number of observations over time presents a significant challenge. Temporal data models, such as factor-adjusted vector autoregressives, are suitable for this type of analysis, as they can capture both high-dimensional correlations and time-varying patterns. A new method for fitting factor-adjusted vector autoregressive models to data is proposed, which employs an alternating strategy of selecting time series components and adjusting factor components in each iteration. A computationally efficient algorithm is developed to estimate the model parameters under a factor structure, and theoretical guarantees are obtained for the method's performance in sparse high-dimensional settings. Additionally, the method is extended to accommodate cases with unknown measurement error variance, missing values, and non-stationary time series, and its performance is demonstrated through simulations and real-world applications in both low and high-dimensional settings. This method is applied to a real-world dataset of high-dimensional temperature and precipitation measurements in the western United States. The proposed method and its performance are compared to other state-of-the-art methods, and results are shown for comprehensive model selection and forecasting.
